title: Openings
description: Opening principles and the main lines of the most popular openings.

steps.text: Three ideas guide every opening: control the center (e4, d4, e5, d5), develop your knights and bishops quickly, and castle to keep your king safe.
Start by taking the center: push your king's pawn two squares.
steps.success: 1.e4 claims the center and opens lines for the queen and bishop.

steps.text: Develop knights before bishops, aim your pieces at the center, and castle early. Avoid moving the same piece twice and don't bring the queen out too soon — it becomes a target.
Black brought the queen out on move two. Why is that usually a bad idea?
choices: The queen can be chased around, costing Black time
Queens can't move on the first move
steps.success: Right — White develops while attacking the queen (for example d4 and Nf3), gaining time.

lessons.title: Italian Game
lessons.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 — fast development, eyes on f7.

steps.text: The Italian Game develops a knight and bishop at once and points the bishop at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
Play the first three moves of the Italian Game as White.
steps.success: That's the Italian Game.

steps.text: Black mirrored with 3…Bc5 (the Giuoco Piano). Prepare d4 with c3, then strike in the center.
steps.success: c3 and d4 build a broad pawn center.

steps.text: Why is f7 a natural target for White in the Italian Game?
steps.success: Exactly — that's why traps like the Fried Liver attack aim at f7.

lessons.title: Ruy Lopez
lessons.summary: The Spanish Game: pressure on e5 through the c6 knight.

steps.text: In the Ruy Lopez, White's bishop attacks the knight that defends e5. It's one of the oldest and deepest openings, played at every level.
Play the main line as White: develop, pin the pressure on c6, keep the bishop when it's attacked, and castle.
steps.hint: e4, Nf3, Bb5, Ba4, then castle.
steps.success: The Morphy Defense main line — White has a lasting initiative.

steps.text: After 3…a6, White retreats 4.Ba4 instead of taking on c6. What's one reason 4.Bxc6 dxc6 5.Nxe5? doesn't win a pawn?
choices: Black answers …Qd4, hitting the knight and e4
steps.success: Correct — the queen fork regains the pawn with a good game.

lessons.title: Queen's Gambit
lessons.summary: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 — a 'gambit' that isn't really a sacrifice.

steps.text: White offers the c-pawn to deflect Black's d5 pawn from the center. If Black takes, White usually wins the pawn back with a strong center.
Play the Queen's Gambit Declined main line as White.
steps.hint: d4, c4, Nc3, then pin the knight with Bg5.
steps.success: Classic QGD — White pins the f6 knight and builds pressure.

steps.text: Black took the pawn: the Queen's Gambit Accepted. Develop calmly; the c4 pawn can't be held.
steps.hint: Knight to f3, open the bishop with e3, then take back on c4.
steps.success: Pawn regained with development, and White keeps a nice center.

steps.text: 2...c6 is the Slav Defense: d5 is supported by a pawn and the c8 bishop stays free. Develop, and when Black takes on c4, stop ...b5.
steps.hint: Both knights out, then a4 once Black captures.
steps.success: a4 stops ...b5 holding the pawn; White will win it back with e3 and Bxc4.

lessons.title: London System
lessons.summary: A reliable setup that works against almost anything.

steps.text: The London System puts the dark-squared bishop on f4 early, then builds a solid triangle of pawns on c3, d4 and e3. It's easy to learn and very hard to break.
Set up the London as White.
steps.success: The London triangle is complete.

lessons.title: Sicilian Defense
lessons.summary: 1…c5 — Black's most popular and combative answer to 1.e4.

steps.text: Instead of copying 1.e4, Black fights for d4 from the side. The positions become unbalanced, giving both sides chances to win.
Play the Najdorf Variation as Black.
steps.hint: c5, d6, take on d4, develop the knight, then …a6.
steps.success: The Najdorf — a favorite of world champions.

steps.text: White's 2.c3 (the Alapin) prepares d4. Strike back in the center at once; your queen is safe on d5 because c3 took that square away from White's knight.
steps.hint: ...d5, recapture with the queen, develop the knight, then pin with the bishop.
steps.success: Free development for Black, and the pin on f3 eyes White's d4 pawn.

steps.text: Black prepares …d5 with …e6, challenging White's e4 pawn. The price: Black's light-squared bishop can get stuck behind the e6 pawn.
Play the Classical French as Black.
steps.hint: e6, d5, then develop the king's knight.
steps.success: Black attacks e4 again and keeps a rock-solid position.

lessons.title: Caro-Kann Defense
lessons.summary: 1…c6 — like the French, but the bishop gets out.

steps.text: The Caro-Kann prepares …d5 with …c6. Black usually develops the light-squared bishop before playing …e6 — so it isn't locked in like in the French.
Play the Classical Caro-Kann as Black.
steps.hint: c6, d5, take on e4, then develop the bishop to f5.
steps.success: The bishop is out — Black is solid and comfortable.

lessons.title: King's Indian Defense
lessons.summary: Let White build a center, then attack it.

steps.text: In the King's Indian, Black fianchettoes the bishop on g7 and castles quickly, inviting White to build a big center — then counterattacks it with …e5 or …c5.
Set up the King's Indian as Black.
steps.hint: Nf6, g6, Bg7, d6, then castle.
steps.success: A fighting setup used by Fischer and Kasparov.

lessons.title: Scotch Game
lessons.summary: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4: open the center at once.

steps.text: The Scotch Game strikes in the center on move three. White swaps the d-pawn for Black's e-pawn and gets free, active piece play. Garry Kasparov made it popular again at the top level.
Play the Scotch as White: open the center on move three and take back with the knight.
steps.hint: e4, Nf3, then d4, and recapture with the knight.
steps.success: That's the Scotch: an open center and a knight on d4.

steps.text: Black attacks e4 with 4...Nf6. Trade on c6, then kick the knight with your e-pawn.
steps.success: The Mieses Variation: White gains space and Black's knight has to move again.

lessons.title: English Opening
lessons.summary: 1.c4: control the center from the side.

steps.text: The English Opening, 1.c4, fights for d5 from the side instead of planting a pawn in the middle. White usually fianchettoes the king's bishop on g2, where it rakes the long diagonal toward Black's queenside.
Play the Four Knights English: develop both knights, fianchetto, and answer ...d5 by trading on d5.
steps.hint: c4, Nc3, Nf3, g3; then take on d5 and bring the bishop to g2.
steps.success: A reversed Sicilian with an extra tempo for White, and the g2 bishop eyes d5.

steps.text: Why does the bishop belong on g2 in the English?
choices: It pressures d5 and the long diagonal
steps.success: Right. From g2 it hits d5, the c6 knight and b7 all at once.
